 A 22% Social Security benefit cut is projected for 2032 if Congress does not act — here's who it would hit, what it could cost and what lawmakers could do
 1 / 12 List slides Social Security's projected 22% cut: 10 things to know before 2032 List slides Previous Start over By Colleen Cabili · Updated November 12, 2026 Add QZ to Google Illustration: Quartz
 Social Security checks could shrink automatically under current law. The program can pay benefits only from money it has. If the reserves behind retirement benefits run out, checks would drop to match the payroll taxes still coming in. There would be no vote in Congress and no advance warning. The reduction would follow from arithmetic alone.
 The 2026 Trustees Report projects that the retirement trust fund could reach that point in 2032, about six years away. The resulting Social Security 22% cut is a projection, not a scheduled event. Lawmakers can still change the outcome, and they have acted on the program's finances before. The size and timing of any cut depend on what Congress does between now and then.
 The cut would reach well beyond people nearing retirement. It would apply across the board, including to people who already collect benefits. For households that rely on a monthly payment for most of their income, the cut would reach the money they live on.
 No single dollar figure shows what a 22% cut would mean for a typical check. A percentage reduction applies to each person's own scheduled benefit. As a result, the dollar loss varies with work history, lifetime earnings and the age at which someone claims.
 One concrete household estimate comes from the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, known as CRFB. The group calculated what the cut would cost a dual-income couple retiring in 2033, and that figure appears later in this list.
 The 10 slides that follow explain the mechanics behind the projection. They cover when the retirement fund is expected to run dry, how the 22% figure is derived and who would feel the cut. They also explain why more money is going out than coming in, what role the disability fund plays and how large the long-range shortfall has grown. Later slides look back at how Congress handled a similar crunch in 1983 and examine raising the payroll tax cap as one way to bring in more money. The final slide turns to planning a retirement budget around the possibility of smaller checks.
 When Social Security's retirement trust fund is projected to run out 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Social Security's retirement trust fund is projected to run out of reserves in 2032, based on the 2026 Trustees Report. Fortune reporter Lena Borrelli laid out what that projection would mean for beneficiaries in a November 2026 article.
 The fund in question is the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance trust fund. It pays retirement benefits, along with benefits to the surviving spouses and children of workers who have died. The 2032 date applies to this fund on its own.
 Running out of reserves does not mean the checks stop. Workers and employers would keep paying payroll taxes, and that money would keep arriving. What would be gone is the cushion: the surplus the program built up in earlier decades.
 The Social Security payroll tax is 12.4% of covered wages. Workers pay 6.2%, and employers match it with another 6.2%. Self-employed people pay the full 12.4% themselves. That stream of revenue is what would remain available to pay benefits after 2032.
 The reserve itself is held in special-issue U.S. Treasury securities. Those bonds earn interest, which counts as income to the fund. Drawing down the reserve means redeeming those bonds to pay benefits. Depletion is the point at which none are left to redeem.
 Social Security has no legal authority to borrow money to cover a gap. Under federal law, it can pay benefits only from incoming revenue and what its trust fund holds. Once the bonds are gone, the program's spending would be limited to what payroll taxes and its other income bring in that year.
 The projection comes from Social Security's board of trustees, which reports to Congress each year. The board includes the secretaries of the Treasury, Labor and Health and Human Services, along with the Social Security commissioner. Each annual report updates the estimate. The depletion year can shift from one report to the next as assumptions about wages, employment, inflation and birth rates change.
 Fortune's headline adds that most Americans are unaware of the projected cut. The 2032 date describes what would happen if lawmakers leave current law unchanged. It is a projection, not a fixed event.
 How the 22% benefit cut figure is calculated 
 Illustration: Quartz
 The 22% figure measures the gap between what Social Security has promised and what it could pay. The 2026 Trustees Report projects that once the retirement trust fund's reserves are exhausted, incoming revenue would cover about 78% of scheduled benefits.
 The rest is subtraction. Full scheduled benefits equal 100%. Take away the 78% that revenue could fund, and 22% is left uncovered. That uncovered share is the size of the projected cut.
 "Scheduled benefits" is the key term in that calculation. It refers to the payments current law promises to every beneficiary. The 78% figure compares the program's expected income with that full promised total. It is a program-wide ratio, not a measure of any single person's check.
 Incoming revenue comes from three main places. The largest is the payroll tax that workers and employers pay on wages. The program also collects federal income tax that some beneficiaries pay on their own benefits. Interest earned on the trust fund's reserves adds a smaller share.
 Those reserves are not a pile of cash. By law, they are invested in special-issue U.S. Treasury securities, which pay interest to the fund. When the securities are redeemed to cover benefits, the reserves shrink. Once they reach zero, the interest income that came with them ends as well.
 The math also explains why the cut would be automatic. Social Security does not keep personal accounts for workers. Payroll taxes collected now pay for benefits going out now. The program has no legal authority to borrow to fill a gap. Without reserves, payments would have to fall to the level that incoming money can support. Fortune summed up the mechanism in its headline: "No vote, no warning, just plain math."
 The 78% figure is a projection, not a fixed number. The trustees, who include the secretary of the Treasury and the Social Security commissioner, are required by law to report to Congress each year. Each report rests on assumptions about wages, employment, birth rates and life expectancy. The 22% estimate reflects the 2026 report's assumptions, and a later report could show a different share.
 Who a Social Security cut would hit, including current retirees 
 Illustration: Quartz
 A projected 22% Social Security cut would not spare people already collecting benefits. It would apply to every beneficiary, from recent retirees to people who have drawn checks for years.
 The reduction would not stop at workers who have yet to file a claim. Checks already arriving each month would shrink as well. That sets an automatic cut apart from a change aimed only at people who have not yet retired.
 The group in that position is large. Social Security sends monthly payments to more than 71 million people.
 For many of them, the program is not a side source of money. Social Security supplies most of the income for 43% of seniors, according to AARP.
 For that group, a cut would land on the largest single piece of what they live on each month. Whatever other income they have makes up the smaller share of their budgets. A reduction in the main source would therefore weigh more heavily than the same cut to a minor one.
 Liner put the stakes for many retirees in plain terms. For them, Liner said, the cut will be "the difference between getting by or not."
 What a 22% cut would cost a dual-income couple retiring in 2033 
 Illustration: Quartz
 The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFB) estimates that a dual-income couple retiring in 2033 would lose about $16,900 a year if the projected Social Security cut takes effect. Spread across 12 months, that comes to roughly $1,400 a month in lost household benefits.
 The figure is an estimate of a possible future loss, not money that has already been taken away. It holds only if Congress leaves current law in place. It also rests on the 2026 Trustees Report's projection that the retirement trust fund will run out of reserves in 2032.
 CRFB framed the loss around a household rather than a single retiree. A couple in which both spouses worked typically collects two benefit checks. A cut that applies to every check would shrink both of them at once. The couple would feel the combined drop in a single household budget.
 The choice of 2033 as the retirement year matters. It falls just after the projected depletion date. Under that timeline, this couple would start collecting after the reduction was already in effect. Their very first payments would arrive at the lower level, with no period of full benefits beforehand.
 That timing separates them from people who retire earlier. Someone who starts collecting before 2032 would first receive full scheduled checks and then see them reduced. The 2033 couple would never receive the full amount under current law.
 The $16,900 figure describes one household type. It is not a per-person number, and it should not be read as the size of a typical single retiree's loss. A single retiree, a one-earner couple or a pair with higher or lower benefits than the couple CRFB modeled would face a different dollar amount.
 What the estimate offers is a sense of scale. For a two-earner household planning to retire shortly after the projected depletion date, the potential gap runs to five figures a year.
 Why the Social Security retirement fund is draining 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Social Security's retirement fund is draining because the program is spending more than it collects. In 2025, costs came to about $1.61 trillion, while income totaled about $1.45 trillion.
 That leaves a one-year gap of roughly $160 billion. The figure is approximate. It comes from subtracting two rounded totals, not from a separately reported number.
 Seen as a ratio, 2025 income covered about 90 cents of every dollar the program paid out. The other 10 cents had to come from somewhere besides that year's revenue.
 That somewhere is the trust fund's reserves. The reserves are money the program collected in earlier years but did not need to spend at the time. When yearly income falls short of yearly costs, Social Security draws on that balance to keep paying full scheduled benefits. Each year that spending runs ahead of income, the balance gets smaller.
 The income side of the ledger has three parts. Most of it comes from payroll taxes that workers and employers pay on wages. Some comes from federal income taxes that certain beneficiaries pay on their benefits. The rest is interest earned on the reserves, which are held in special-issue U.S. Treasury securities. As the reserves shrink, the interest they generate shrinks with them.
 The cost side reflects the size of the program. Social Security sends monthly payments to more than 71 million people. Those checks go out every month, and the total grows as more people claim benefits.
 Benefit amounts follow a set formula tied to each worker's earnings record. They do not shrink when a year's revenue comes in light.
 The imbalance is what turns a funding gap into a deadline. A program that took in more than it spent could keep adding to its reserves. A program that spends more than it takes in can cover the difference only as long as its savings last.
 The disability trust fund and the option to merge the two funds 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Social Security pays benefits from two legally separate trust funds, and combining them is one option Congress could use to delay an automatic cut to retirement checks. A merger would not bring in any new money.
 The Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund covers retirees and survivors. The Disability Insurance Trust Fund covers disabled workers.
 The disability fund pays monthly benefits to workers who can no longer hold a job because of a qualifying disability. It also pays certain members of their families. These payments are commonly known as SSDI, short for Social Security Disability Insurance. Like the retirement fund, the disability fund is financed mainly by payroll taxes on wages.
 The combined Social Security payroll tax rate is 12.4%. Workers pay 6.2% of covered wages, and employers pay a matching 6.2%. Federal law sets how much of that rate flows into each fund.
 Under current law, a surplus in one fund cannot cover a shortfall in the other. Moving money between them takes an act of Congress.
 Congress has done this before. The Bipartisan Budget Act of 2015 temporarily shifted a larger share of the payroll tax to the disability fund. At the time, that fund was projected to run dry in 2016. The reallocation covered 2016 through 2018, and the earlier split returned in 2019. A 1994 law had also moved a larger share of the tax toward disability benefits.
 The Social Security trustees also publish a combined projection that treats both funds as a single pool. That figure is hypothetical. It shows how long the program could pay full scheduled benefits if the reserves were legally merged.
 A merger or reallocation changes the timing of a shortfall, not its size. It spreads existing reserves across both programs without raising revenue or lowering costs. Any money shifted toward retirement benefits would come out of the reserves that support disability payments.
 Social Security's 75-year funding gap of $29.3 trillion 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Social Security's long-range funding gap now stands at $29.3 trillion, measured over the next 75 years. That figure is up from $25.1 trillion, an increase of $4.2 trillion.
 The increase works out to a rise of about 17% from the earlier figure. The shortfall widened between estimates. A fix sized to close the older $25.1 trillion gap would now leave part of the problem unsolved.
 The gap measures the distance between two projections. One is the total of benefits the program is scheduled to pay over the 75-year period. The other is the money the program is expected to collect over the same span. The $29.3 trillion figure is what remains when the second is subtracted from the first.
 Both sides of that calculation are projections, so the gap moves when assumptions change. The jump from the earlier estimate shows that the number shifts from one report to the next rather than staying fixed.
 The Social Security trustees use a 75-year window as their standard test of the program's long-term finances. The period is long enough to cover the working and retirement years of nearly everyone paying into the system today. It reaches far beyond any single trust fund date.
 That makes the long-range gap a separate question from the projected 2032 depletion of the retirement trust fund. The depletion date marks when reserves would run out. The 75-year gap measures how far scheduled benefits outrun projected revenue across several decades.
 A change that pushes the depletion date later does not by itself close the long-range gap. A measure that adds revenue or trims costs for only a few years would leave much of the 75-year shortfall in place. A durable solution would have to hold up across decades of future payments.
 For someone estimating a future check, the size of the gap indicates how much any eventual fix would need to cover. Without congressional action, the projections show scheduled benefits outrunning expected revenue across the 75-year window.
 How Congress fixed the 1983 Social Security crisis 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Congress resolved Social Security's last near-insolvency with the Social Security Amendments of 1983, which President Ronald Reagan signed on April 20, 1983. The law paired tax increases with benefit reductions and spread the cost across workers, retirees and employers.
 The crisis had been building for years. By the early 1980s, the retirement program's reserves had fallen low enough to put full, on-time benefit payments in doubt. Lawmakers could not agree on a fix through ordinary legislative channels.
 Reagan responded in December 1981 by appointing the National Commission on Social Security Reform. Alan Greenspan, who later became chair of the Federal Reserve, led the 15-member panel. Its members came from both parties. The commission delivered its recommendations in January 1983. Congress passed a package built largely on them within a few months.
 One central change was a higher full retirement age. The law raised it gradually from 65 to 67. The phase-in began with people born in 1938 and reached 67 for those born in 1960 or later. The long schedule meant no one close to retirement in 1983 faced a sudden shift.
 The package also made Social Security benefits taxable income for the first time. Up to half of benefits became subject to federal income tax for individuals with income above $25,000 and couples above $32,000. Those thresholds were never indexed to inflation. As a result, they now apply to far more retirees than they did in 1983.
 Retirees also absorbed a six-month delay in their annual cost-of-living adjustment. On the revenue side, the law moved up payroll tax increases already scheduled under earlier legislation. It also raised the rate paid by self-employed workers.
 Coverage expanded as well. Federal employees hired on or after Jan. 1, 1984, were brought into Social Security, adding new payroll tax contributors. The same law covered members of Congress and the president. It also made coverage mandatory for employees of nonprofit organizations.
 The 1983 law is the most recent precedent for a Social Security funding cliff of this kind. Congress legislated before benefits were cut automatically. No single change carried the full burden of that fix.
 Raising the Social Security payroll tax cap as a funding fix 
 Illustration: Quartz
 The Social Security payroll tax applies only to wages up to a yearly cap, and changing that cap is one lever Congress could use to bring in more revenue. The cap is $184,500 in 2026 and is set to rise to $192,300 in 2027.
 Workers pay 6.2% of covered wages into Social Security. Employers match that share, for a combined rate of 12.4%. Self-employed people pay the full 12.4% themselves on net earnings up to the same cap.
 Pay above the cap owes no Social Security tax. A worker whose earnings pass the cap partway through the year stops paying the tax on the rest of that year's wages. A worker earning at least $184,500 in 2026 pays $11,439 in Social Security tax for the year, and the employer pays the same amount.
 Each employer withholds the tax up to the cap on its own. A person with two jobs whose combined wages top the cap can end up overpaying. That worker can claim the excess as a credit on a federal income tax return.
 The cap is not fixed in law as a single dollar amount. It is adjusted each year in line with the national average wage index. The scheduled move from 2026 to 2027 lifts it by $7,800. The Social Security Administration officially calls the cap the contribution and benefit base. It announces each new figure in October, alongside the annual cost-of-living adjustment.
 The cap also shapes what workers get back. Benefits are calculated from earnings up to the cap. Wages above it neither add to the tax bill nor count toward a future check. Any proposal to raise or remove the cap has to settle whether those newly taxed earnings would also raise benefits.
 Medicare works differently. Workers and employers each pay 1.45% for Medicare's hospital insurance tax, a combined 2.9% that applies to all wages with no ceiling. Employers also withhold an additional 0.9% Medicare tax on an employee's wages above $200,000.
 How to plan your retirement budget for a possible benefit cut 
 Illustration: Quartz
 One practical way to prepare for a possible Social Security cut is to build a second retirement budget. In that version, your benefit covers about 78% of the scheduled amount.
 That share is what incoming revenue is projected to pay once the retirement trust fund's reserves are gone. The 2026 Trustees Report projects that point for 2032.
 The starting point is your own scheduled benefit. The Social Security Administration publishes each worker's estimated benefit in a personal statement. That statement is available through a my Social Security account on the agency's website.
 Married households need one estimate per spouse. Each person's benefit would shrink by the same share. The second budget should therefore apply the lower figure to both checks, not just one.
 With that estimate in hand, the comparison is direct. One budget uses the full scheduled benefit. The other uses roughly 78% of it. The difference between the two is the monthly amount that savings, pension income or earnings from work would need to cover if the reduction takes effect.
 Claiming age affects how long the full amount would last. Under the current projection, someone who starts benefits before 2032 would receive full checks until the reserves run out. After that, those checks would drop. Someone who first claims after that point would start at the lower level.
 The second budget is a stress test, not a forecast. The reduction would happen only if Congress does not change the program's finances before the reserves are depleted. The 2032 date is itself a projection. Later Trustees Reports can move it earlier or later.
 That makes the comparison worth repeating each year. The trustees issue a new report annually. A worker's personal statement also changes as new earnings are added to the record.
 For a household that depends on Social Security for most of its income, the gap between the two budgets is the number to track. If other income cannot cover that gap, the reduced budget shows which monthly expenses would need to shrink.
